question.text:
Consider the system of linear equations

\[ \begin{cases} 2x-y=-6 \\ \, \, \, x+ y= 7. \end{cases} \]

According to Cramer's rule, the unknown $y$ can be written as $y = \dfrac{D_y}{ \begin{vmatrix} 2 & \!\!-1 \\ 1 & 1\end{vmatrix}}$, where $D_y=$
question.explanation:
We are given the system \[ \begin{cases} 2x-y=\color{blue}-6 \\ \, \, \, x+ y= {\color{blue}7}. \end{cases} \]

The determinant of the coefficient matrix is \[ \begin{align*} D &=\begin{vmatrix} 2& \!\!-1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{vmatrix}. \\ \end{align*} \]

Now, to construct $D_y$, we replace the second column of the coefficient matrix by the right-hand side column of the given system: \[ \begin{align*} D_{y} &=\begin{vmatrix} 2 & \!\!\color{blue}-6 \\ 1 & \color{blue}7 \end{vmatrix} \\ \end{align*} \]

exampleAnswers.title: Solving for a Coefficient in a 2x2 Linear System Using Cramer's Rule

question.text:
Let $\langle x,3 \rangle$ be the solution of the system of equations below. \[ \begin{cases} 2x+3y=10 \\ kx-4y=12. \end{cases} \] Which of the following equations could be solved to find the value of $k?$

  1. $3 \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ k & -4 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 10\\ k & 12 \end{vmatrix}$
  2. $\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ k & -4 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 10\\ k & 12 \end{vmatrix}$
  3. $\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ k & -4 \end{vmatrix} = 3 \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 10\\ k & 12 \end{vmatrix}$
question.explanation:
The determinant of the coefficient matrix is

\begin{align*} D &=\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ k & -4 \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $y$ is given by $y=\dfrac{D_y}{D},$ where

\begin{align*} D_{y} &=\begin{vmatrix} 2 & 10\\ k & 12 \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

Therefore:

\begin{align*} y & = \dfrac{D_y}{D} \\[5pt] 3 &= \dfrac { \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 10\\ k & 12 \end{vmatrix} } { \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ k & -4 \end{vmatrix} } \\[5pt] 3 \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ k & -4 \end{vmatrix} &= \begin{vmatrix} 2 & 10\\ k & 12 \end{vmatrix} \end{align*}

So, the correct answer is "I only".

example.title: Solving for a Coefficient in a 2x2 Linear System Using Cramer's Rule

question.text:
Let $\langle x,-2 \rangle$ be the solution of the system of equations below. \[ \begin{cases} x-y= 2 \\ 2x+y=k \end{cases} \] Which of the following equations could be solved to find the value of $k?$

  1. $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & k \end{vmatrix} = -6$
  2. $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & k \end{vmatrix} = -12$
  3. $\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & k \end{vmatrix} = 3$
question.explanation:
The determinant of the coefficient matrix is

\begin{align*} D &= \begin{vmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 1 + 2 \\[5pt] &= 3. \end{align*}

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $y$ is given by $y=\dfrac{D_y}{D},$ where \begin{align} D_y &= \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & k \end{vmatrix}. \end{align}

Therefore:

\begin{align*} y &= \dfrac{D_y}{D} \\[5pt] -2 &= \dfrac{\begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & k \end{vmatrix}}{3} \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & k \end{vmatrix} &= -6 \end{align*}

So, the correct answer is "I only".

example.title: Solving for a Coefficient in a 2x2 Linear System Using Cramer's Rule

question.text:
Let $\langle x,1 \rangle$ be the solution of the system of equations below. \[ \begin{cases} 3x-y= k \\ x+4y=3 \end{cases} \] Which of the following equations could be solved to find the value of $k?$

  1. $\begin{vmatrix} 3 & k \\ 1 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 5$
  2. $\begin{vmatrix} 3 & k \\ 1 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = -7$
  3. $\begin{vmatrix} 3 & k \\ 1 & 3 \end{vmatrix} = 13$
question.explanation:
The determinant of the coefficient matrix is

\begin{align*} D &= \begin{vmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ 1 & 4 \end{vmatrix} \\[5pt] &= 12 + 1 \\[5pt] &= 13. \end{align*}

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $y$ is given by $y=\dfrac{D_y}{D},$ where \begin{align} D_y &= \begin{vmatrix} 3 & k \\ 1 & 3 \end{vmatrix}. \end{align}

Therefore:

\begin{align*} 1 &= \dfrac{D_y}{D} \\[5pt] 1 &= \dfrac{\begin{vmatrix} 3 & k \\ 1 & 3 \end{vmatrix}}{13} \\[5pt] \begin{vmatrix} 3 & k \\ 1 & 3 \end{vmatrix} &= 13 \end{align*}

So, the correct answer is "III only".

question.text:
Let $\langle 2, y \rangle$ be the solution of the system of equations below.

\[ \begin{cases} 4x + ky = 5 \\ x + 2y = -4 \end{cases} \]

Which of the following equations could be solved to find the value of $k?$

  1. $\begin{vmatrix} 4 & k \\ 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} 5 & k \\ -4 & 2 \end{vmatrix} $
  2. $2\begin{vmatrix} 4 & k \\ 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} 5 & k \\ -4 & 2 \end{vmatrix}$
  3. $\begin{vmatrix} 4 & k \\ 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} = 2\begin{vmatrix} 5 & k \\ -4 & 2 \end{vmatrix}$
question.explanation:
The determinant of the coefficient matrix is

\[ \begin{align*} D &= \begin{vmatrix} 4 & k \\ 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*} \]

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $x$ is given by $x=\dfrac{D_x}{D},$ where

\[ \begin{align*} D_x &= {\begin{vmatrix} 5 & k \\ -4 & 2 \end{vmatrix}}. \end{align*} \]

Therefore: \[ \begin{align*} x &= \dfrac{D_x}{D}\\[5pt] 2 &= \dfrac{\begin{vmatrix} 5 & k \\ -4 & 2 \end{vmatrix}}{\begin{vmatrix} 4 & k \\ 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix}}\\[5pt] 2 \begin{vmatrix} 4 & k \\ 1 & 2 \end{vmatrix} &= \begin{vmatrix} 5 & k \\ -4 & 2 \end{vmatrix} \end{align*} \]

So, the correct answer is "II only".

example.title: Solving for a Coefficient in a 2x2 Linear System Using Cramer's Rule

question.text:
Let $\langle x,-2 \rangle$ be the solution of the system of equations below. \[ \begin{cases} 15x+8y=-1 \\ kx+13y=-31. \end{cases} \] Which of the following equations could be solved to find the value of $k?$

  1. $\begin{vmatrix}15 & 8 \\k & 13\end{vmatrix} =2\begin{vmatrix}15 & -1\\k & -31 \end{vmatrix}$
  2. $ \begin{vmatrix}15 & 8 \\k & 13\end{vmatrix} =-4\begin{vmatrix}15 & -1\\k & -31 \end{vmatrix}$
  3. $-2 \begin{vmatrix}15 & 8 \\k & 13\end{vmatrix} =\begin{vmatrix}15 & -1\\k & -31 \end{vmatrix}$
question.explanation:
The determinant of the coefficient matrix is

\begin{align*} D &=\begin{vmatrix} 15 & 8 \\ k & 13 \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

According to Cramer's rule, the value of $y$ is given by $y=\dfrac{D_y}{D},$ where

\begin{align*} D_{y} &=\begin{vmatrix} 15 & -1\\ k & -31 \end{vmatrix}. \end{align*}

Therefore:

\begin{align*} y & = \dfrac{D_y}{D} \\[5pt] -2 &= \dfrac { \begin{vmatrix} 15 & -1\\ k & -31 \end{vmatrix} } { \begin{vmatrix} 15 & 8 \\ k & 13 \end{vmatrix} } \\[5pt] -2 \begin{vmatrix} 15 & 8 \\ k & 13 \end{vmatrix} &= \begin{vmatrix} 15 & -1\\ k & -31 \end{vmatrix} \end{align*}

So, the correct answer is "III only".
